title: Burned Cars, Anti-Immigrant Riots, and India's T20I Tour of Belfast Hanging by a Thread
excerpt: The BCCI is monitoring escalating violence in Northern Ireland as Cricket Ireland weighs whether to relocate the June 26-28 matches. For the Indian community in Belfast, the stakes go beyond cricket.
body:
The last time India played cricket in Belfast, it was 2007. Nineteen years later, the Men in Blue were supposed to return to Stormont Cricket Ground for a two-match T20I series on June 26 and 28. Instead, the city has spent the past week burning.

A knife attack by a 30-year-old Sudanese asylum seeker, which left a local man blinded, ignited a firestorm of anti-immigrant protests across Northern Ireland. What began as peaceful demonstrations escalated into full-blown riots. Up to 300 protesters have set fire to cars, trucks, and shops near Belfast. Police deployed water cannons. Sixteen arrests have been made. At least 12 officers have been injured.

Cricket Ireland has taken notice. In an official statement, the board said it was "continuing to monitor the situation" and would decide on domestic fixtures within 48 hours. "The safety and security of players, coaches, match officials, and supporters is paramount," the statement read.

The BCCI, according to a report by Dainik Jagran, is also watching closely. A source told the newspaper that the safety of players and coaching staff is the top priority. If normalcy does not return before India's arrival, the matches could be relocated — though the final call rests with Cricket Ireland.

## What Is at Stake

The Ireland tour is more than a warm-up. For Shreyas Iyer, it would be his first assignment as India's T20I captain, having been named to lead a squad that includes Abhishek Sharma, Sanju Samson, Tilak Varma, and Axar Patel. For 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, it would be his senior international debut — a moment the cricketing world has been anticipating since his explosive IPL performances.

Ireland's cricket board, meanwhile, has a different kind of pressure. Hosting India is the single most lucrative fixture on Cricket Ireland's calendar. Losing it — or seeing it relocated to Dublin's Malahide, where India last played in 2023 — would be a financial blow that the board can ill afford.

## The Diaspora Dimension

For the Indian community in Northern Ireland, the unrest carries a weight that transcends sport. While the protests have not specifically targeted Indians, the community has faced racist attacks in the past. The anti-immigrant tenor of the demonstrations has put many on edge.

Indians living in Belfast and across Northern Ireland — many of them healthcare workers, IT professionals, and students who arrived over the past decade — are watching the situation with concern. Community organisations have urged caution while emphasising that the violence is not directed at any one group.

But the optics of an Indian cricket team arriving in a city still smouldering from riots would be uncomfortable for everyone involved. The BCCI has historically been conservative on security matters, pulling out of tours or demanding relocation when it deems the risk unacceptable.

## What Happens Next

Cricket Ireland is expected to make a decision on local fixtures first, which could signal the direction for the India series. The matches are still two weeks away, leaving a narrow window for the situation to stabilise.

If Belfast is ruled out, Malahide — which successfully hosted India's previous visits — remains the obvious alternative. A venue change would preserve the series without forcing a cancellation, something neither board wants.

For now, the Indian squad is focused on the ongoing ODI series against Afghanistan in Dharamsala. But somewhere in the planning rooms of Mumbai and Dublin, contingency calls are being made. The question is no longer whether India will tour Ireland. It is where.
